summary: Describes the architecture for a protocol that manages the lifecycle of Trusted Applications inside a Trusted Execution Environment, a protected area where code and data cannot be tampered with or read from outside. It explains the motivation and the roles involved.

eli5.summary: A locked safe inside a computer where special programs run. This explains how to put programs in and update them safely.

subtitle: How to securely install and manage trusted programs inside a protected computer enclave.

tldr.problem: Trusted Execution Environments protect code and data from tampering, but they come in many different hardware variants. How can software developers deliver trusted applications to different TEE types, and how can device administrators install and update them safely?
tldr.mechanism: The TEEP architecture defines roles (TAM, TEEP Agent, TEEP Broker, developer) and protocols for a Trusted Application Manager to verify device capabilities, authenticate itself, and deliver signed trusted applications with personalized configuration data.
tldr.outcome: A standardized protocol for lifecycle management allows a single trusted application to work across devices with different TEE types, as long as each TEE trusts the same manager. This enables scalable deployment of security-sensitive code.

today: RFC 9397 is an Informational document describing the TEEP architecture. It has not been obsoleted. Companion protocol specifications (such as RFC 9397 companion RFCs) define the actual TEEP protocol messages and bindings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a protected area where code runs isolated from the main operating system and cannot be tampered with or read from outside, even by the OS. TEEs protect sensitive operations like payment processing, biometric authentication, and data encryption.

However, TEEs come from different vendors with different designs: Intel SGX, Arm TrustZone, AMD SEV, and others. Installing and updating code inside a TEE requires vendor-specific mechanisms. This RFC defines a common architecture and protocol so that developers can deploy trusted applications across multiple TEE types.

The TEEP protocol handles the lifecycle of trusted applications: installation, verification, personalization with device-specific secrets, and removal.
sections.eli5: Different computers have different kinds of locked safes. This explains a way to manage programs in any safe, using a trusted manager that both your computer and the developer trust.

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.content:
Five main roles work together in TEEP:

Trusted Application Manager (TAM): A remote service that developers trust and devices authorize to manage trusted applications. A TAM holds the developer's signed trusted applications and sends them to devices on request.

TEEP Agent: Code running inside the TEE on the device. It receives requests from the TAM, verifies the TAM's identity, and installs or removes trusted applications.

TEEP Broker: Code running in the normal OS on the device. The TEE cannot access the network directly, so the Broker relays messages between the TEEP Agent and the TAM over the internet.

Device Administrator: The person or enterprise managing the device. They control which TAMs are trusted and can approve or reject trusted applications.

Trusted Component Signer: The developer. They sign their trusted applications with a key that the TEE recognizes as authorized.
sections.eli5: A developer writes a secret program and signs it. A trusted manager (TAM) holds it. Your computer's broker asks the manager to send it. The safe inside checks the signature, then runs it.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
Payment: A mobile payment application stores cryptographic keys and biometric data in a TEE. The trusted application processes the payment, and only the TEEP protocol can update it to fix security issues.

Authentication: A TEE stores authentication keys and limits access to them through a well-defined interface, protecting them from malware in the main OS.

IoT Security: IoT devices in untrusted locations (ATMs, vending machines, field sensors) use a TEE to prevent malware from controlling actuators or stealing credentials.

Confidential Cloud Computing: A tenant rents a server in a cloud data center and uses the server's TEE to run code that the cloud provider cannot see or modify, protecting sensitive data from the hosting provider.
sections.eli5: You can use a safe inside a computer to protect payments, login keys, IoT devices that might be stolen, or cloud data from snooping by the hosting company.

sections.title: Trust and Keys
sections.content:
The architecture relies on digital certificates and keys. Each TEE has a unique key pair generated by the manufacturer and burned into the hardware. The TEE uses this key to sign responses to a TAM, proving it is the real device.

Each TAM has a key pair and certificate that the TEE pre-trusts (or trusts through a certificate chain). When the TAM sends a request, it signs with its private key. The TEE verifies the signature and checks that the TAM's certificate chains up to a trusted root.

Developers sign their trusted applications with a key that the TEE recognizes as authorized (pre-installed or updated through TEEP). Only signed applications can run.

Device Administrators can update the list of trusted TAMs and developers on their devices by managing the trust anchor stores in the TEE.
sections.eli5: The TEE holds a secret key only the manufacturer knows. The TAM has a key the TEE trusts. Developers sign their programs. Everyone checks signatures to make sure no one is lying.

sections.title: Delivery and Installation
sections.content:
A developer builds two applications: an untrusted application (UA) in the normal OS and a trusted application (TA) in the TEE. The developer signs the TA with a key the TEE trusts.

The developer can bundle the TA with the UA, or ship the TA through a TAM to be installed later. When a user installs the UA from an app store, the UA may ask a TEEP Broker to fetch the TA from the TAM.

The TEEP Broker passes a request to the TEEP Agent. The Agent checks whether the TA is needed, contacts a trusted TAM from a list, receives the TA, verifies the signature, and installs it in the TEE.

The TA may also require Personalization Data unique to the device or user (encryption keys, configuration, account information). This data is encrypted with a key unique to that TEE before being sent, so the network and even the Broker cannot read it.
sections.eli5: An app asks to install its secret part. The phone's broker contacts a trusted manager. The manager sends the secret code and custom data. The safe inside checks the signature and installs it.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A single TA can be deployed across devices with different TEE types, as long as each TEE type is supported and each device trusts the same TAM. Device manufacturers or Device Administrators can install a TAM's public key or certificate into the device's trust anchor store.

Some devices may have multiple TEEs. In this case, the device may use one TEEP Broker for all TEEs or multiple Brokers, one per TEE. Each TEE runs its own TEEP Agent and has its own trust configuration.

The TEEP architecture does not mandate a single TAM. Devices can trust multiple TAMs, and a developer can use multiple TAMs to reach devices from different manufacturers or carriers.

Updates to trusted applications must be handled carefully, since other applications may depend on them. A SUIT manifest (Software Update for Internet of Things format) expresses dependencies and installation steps.
sections.eli5: Many devices with different safes can trust the same manager. One developer can reach them all. Managers can update programs without breaking other apps that depend on them.
